title: Coalmine reopens despite previous owners saying royalties made it unprofitable
text:
A Queensland mining company has employed 275 workers and reopened a Bowen Basin coalmine that went into receivership in 2025.

Argo Resources Queensland purchased the New Burton Mine near Moranbah, about 120 kilometres south-west of Mackay, from Bowen Coking Coal in June.

It is the fourth mine Argo has a controlling interest in after acquiring a 70 per cent stake in Bowen Basin mines Broadlea, Carborough Downs and Ironbark in March for an undisclosed sum.

Premier David Crisafulli reopened the mine today, saying coal mining had a "bullish future".

"People need to know that the future of mining in Queensland is secure," Mr Crisafulli said.

"But also, the future of coal mining in Queensland, and I'm talking about both thermal and met [metallurgical] coal, there's a future for both."

David Crisafulli visits the mine for its reopening. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

He said the Queensland government had not contributed to the mine with financial incentives or delayed royalty payments.

"Queensland taxpayers, not only will they not be out of pocket one cent because of this, they'll be the net beneficiary because the royalties are being paid and they're being paid in full," he said.

Royalties no barrier

Argo CEO Richard Livingstone-Blevins said royalties were not a deterrent to acquiring coalmines.

"At the end of the day, we invested in the state based on the current royalty regime that's in place," he said.

The mine entrance near Moranbah in the Bowen Basin. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

Mr Livingstone-Blevins declined to comment on why the previous mine owners were not profitable.

"We've got great infrastructure, we've got great people, we've got coal on the ground at economic strip ratios, and we've got a lot of ground that we can open up, moving forward," he said.

"We all run vastly different businesses with vastly different cost profiles and different assets that have different operating costs."

Mr Livingstone-Blevins said Argo planned to mine 10 million tonnes of saleable coal by 2028.

"We have two prep plant hubs, we've got two rail loops, we're serviced by our own haul road, we've got our own camp, we've got four mines along the strike, and we've got over 4 billion tonnes of resource in the ground, which we seek to develop as we push forward," he said.

title: Victorian Big Build inquiry rebukes agencies on redactions
text:
A former advisor to ex-premier Daniel Andrews is among public servants accused by Victoria's Big Build royal commissioner of delaying his inquiry and flouting their legal obligations.

At the royal commission into alleged corruption on major public projects today, counsel assisting Chris Young KC said the inquiry was being thwarted by heavy redactions and last-minute submissions of key evidence.

Just two days ago, he said, the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority (VIDA) told to the commission about text messages in 2022 from senior public servants directly concerning work stoppages and the CFMEU at a level crossing removal project in Sunbury the commission has been investigating all week.

"Those messages included reference to the PPO, which we understand to be a reference to the premier's private office, and some named individuals," Mr Young said.

Counsel assisting the commission Chris Young KC said the poor disclosure by a government entity defied what Premier Ben Carroll said the inquiry was set up to do. (Supplied)

"Steps are now being taken to secure evidence from those persons.

"I am not tendering those text messages now, but we will."

The messages were from Matt Toner, direct adviser to Andrews, and from Matthew Phelan, chief of staff to the director general of VIDA, Corey Hannett.

Mr Young said Mr Toner left his role under Mr Andrews some time in 2024.

Daniel Andrews was premier of Victoria during most of the periods of time under investigation at the royal commission this week. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

"Around the time he left that position as an advisor to the premier he was referred to in notes of a delegates meeting at the CFMEU," he said.

Former Victorian secretary of the CFMEU John Setka described Mr Toner during that meeting as "a good asset to the union", he said.

The inquiry also heard a notebook belonging to government executive Evan Tattersall, was submitted by VIDA prior to the public hearings with all its pages blacked out.

A photo of two pages of Evan Tattersall's notebook submitted by the government's Big Build authority to the Royal Commission. Every page submitted was blacked-out like this until the authority re-submitted at the commissioner's request. (Supplied)

Just this morning, as hearings were already underway, VIDA submitted a much less redacted version, after being compelled to do so, Mr Young said. The notes are about the same Sunbury level crossing project.

He also said there were other VIDA documents the commission had requested, which the agency had failed to submit.

"It is profoundly disappointing in light of everything that's been said by the premier of this state [Ben Carroll] about the importance of this commission, about the importance of its work, and about the cooperation it would receive from the state, that state entities — senior, current and former state officers and employees — only engage with this commission when compelled to do so and seem otherwise content to do nothing," Mr Young said.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis said late provision of information from government individuals and entities had "disrupted the orderly investigation" of the inquiry.

Commissioner Chris Kourakis issued words of advice to government employees required to disclose information to the inquiry: "if in doubt, send it out". (Supplied)

"I encourage, in the strongest terms, early, genuine and comprehensive disclosure, by all serving or former ministers and public servants, and their advisors," he said.

"A working rule along the lines 'if in doubt send it out' will also allow the recipient to meet their legal obligations to provide the information within the stipulated time."

Counsel assisting VIDA Richard Knowles apologised and said the agency would respond to the commission's requests as soon as possible.

John Holland leadership 'at the mercy' of CFMEU, commission hears

The royal commission today also heard from several executives from construction firm John Holland and CPB contractors today, quizzing them on their dealings with the CFMEU in the civil (road and rail) projects.

Industrial relations general manager for John Holland, Trent Smith, told the commission by mid-2021 the business acknowledged it could only survive in Victoria if it formed an enterprise agreement for civil projects with the CFMEU.

Mr Smith said by that stage, a "hostile" relationship with the CFMEU was "touching all parts of our business".

John Holland executive Trent Smith said the company's leadership came to the view that cooperating with the CFMEU was critical to winning state government work. (Supplied)

He said it was a widely-held belief across the firm that the CFMEU had influence within the state government, compared to the alternative union for civil projects, the Australian Workers' Union.

"That's how we understood the relationship to be…it was a very clear position within John Holland," he said.

Therefore, engagement with the CFMEU became part of the company's broader strategy to "better position our business with the state government", he said.

Senior executives from contractor John Holland have given evidence a work stoppage at the Gap Road Sunbury level crossing project in 2022 caused by the CFMEU was threatening their ability to deliver the project. (Supplied: Victorian government)

John Holland signed an enterprise bargaining agreement with the union in August 2021.

Mr Smith said this was largely a symbolic gesture by then, given the company was already "at [the CFMEU's] mercy" via sub-contracted labour aligned with that union.

Senior civil engineer for John Holland, Wayne Donnelly, told the commission the work stoppage in June 2022 on the Sunbury level crossing was causing concern of major cost blowout, because of delays.

By April 2022, 95 per cent of civil contractors in Victoria had an enterprise agreement in place with the CFMEU, the commission heard.

title: A coffee cart and the Finnish embassy gain more traction than Albanese
text:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Anthony Albanese and his government could only wish for the type of cut-through the Finnish embassy in Canberra received when it temporarily closed on Tuesday.

It all started when Finland's ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea, starred in a video on Instagram promoting a campaign to fly singles from around the world to Helsinki for dinner dates.

"Are you single? Good. We are here to help … maybe the problem is not you, it's your postcode," he said.

Loading Instagram content

The post's popularity created the perfect storm for the embassy's next message to followers, an innocuous reminder the building would be closed for a planning day, to be sent out to the masses.

An unexpected viral hit was born. People across the world shared their concern about the embassy's one-day closure.

"Bad day to be a Finnish embassy in Canberra enthusiast," one person commented.

The Canberra Raiders, travel company Contiki and video game Angry Birds also chimed in. Haapea filmed a ribbon cutting for the building's grand re-opening the next day.

Even Finland's President Alexander Stubb joined in. On the sidelines of the United Nations climate summit in Türkiye, he shared a happy snap of himself with Albanese.

"I have confirmed to … Albanese that the Finnish embassy in Canberra is open," he wrote.

PM gets busy

Perhaps conscious of the optics of a second week abroad, Albanese packed a lot into his couple of days at home after returning from the Caribbean last week.

He attended a Nepal Festival in Sydney, reversed his decision to sell off four historic defence sites, and announced new mandatory safety and security standards for artificial intelligence.

The prime minister's departure was delayed by a day, meaning he was able to be there in person to chair a meeting of the expenditure review committee ahead of next month's Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

A string of interest rate rises and sticky inflation has ramped up pressure on the government to find savings. There is speculation that low-hanging fruit such as the electric vehicle and home battery subsidies could be targeted.

The government argues the schemes promote Australia's transition to renewables, but both are as expensive as they are enormously popular.

Costs have blown out beyond initial projections, and the government has already committed to partially winding back EV subsidies next year following changes already made to the home batteries scheme.

Of course, in the backdrop of all of this are the rumours around the future of Jim Chalmers.

The relationship between the treasurer and Albanese has been the subject of many newspaper articles in recent weeks, as a usually united caucus vented frustrations publicly, with unnamed sources suggesting Chalmers should be replaced.

Speculation about the relationship between the prime minister and his treasurer has ramped up in recent weeks. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

This week, Environment Minister Murray Watt was asked if he'd like to see an end to the "undermining and leaking" against the treasurer.

"Yes, I would," he replied. "As a member of a government, I take seriously the responsibility to work together, to support government policies, and also to get out there and support each other in what, at times, are very difficult times."

Ahead of his departure for Türkiye, Albanese said "yes" when asked if it was his preference that Chalmers remained Treasurer until the next election.

"The treasurer is doing a great job," he said as he dismissed concerns the good ship government had sprung one too many leaks.

Loading

A side of coffee with your COP?

Albanese may have delayed the departure for his 11-day trip covering three international summits, but that didn't eat too much into his itinerary.

Much like any regular Aussie making a trip across the world, the prime minister (and his team) arrived at dawn and hit the ground running. He almost immediately attended the leaders' summit at COP31, the United Nations Climate Change Conference.

Australia had pushed hard to host the summit in Adelaide but conceded to Türkiye, taking on the compromised position to oversee negotiations and host a pre-COP event in the Pacific.

COP31 summit targets major electrification push The climate summit will push for nations around the world to electrify their energy faster and move away from fossil fuels.

It's Albanese's first-time attending COP as prime minister. He used his opening address to argue that other nations should step up their climate actions and support vulnerable nations, such as those in the Pacific.

Australia and Türkiye want the summit to conclude with agreements on electrification, climate finance and adaption.

Albanese pointed to the strong uptake of home batteries in the past year (backed by the aforementioned subsidy) as Australia's credentials for being a climate leader.

But United Nations secretary-general António Guterres called for more than just words.

"We must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it and delivering it," he said.

Fossil fuels, Guterres said, must "go the way of the dinosaurs" as he urged governments not to invest in any new coal developments — something Pacific nations have been critical of the Albanese government for.

Meanwhile, Australia's pavilion at the event has proven to be quite the drawcard. Why? Because of the taxpayer-funded coffee cart.

Australia's coffee station has proved to be enormously popular at COP. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

As Clare Armstrong, who is on the ground for the ABC, observed, the baristas can't get the flat whites out fast enough — with some willing to wait for more than an hour.

It's probably no surprise that the $32,000 price tag for the coffee hub drew criticism from the opposition. That's despite the idea harking back to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor's time as energy minister.

But if you ask former PM Malcolm Turnbull, who is also at COP, it's all about giving people a taste of what Australia has to offer.

"All the dollars that are spent on marketing here, that is probably the best dollar spent," he said.

title: Hunt is on for heir to strange block of land
text:
Local sleuths and state bureaucrats are trying to find the true heir to a strange block of land in Logan, south of Brisbane, with only five days left.

The Department of Transport and Main Roads is looking for anyone who believes they have an interest in the August Thorsborne estate.

That tiny block of land, 16 metres long and 60 centimetres wide, is needed to facilitate upgrades to the Holmview station precinct, which is part of Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail.

A published Notice of Intention to Resume states:

"To: The beneficiaries, heirs or any party establishing an interest in the estate of August Thorsborne (deceased) Take notice that on 13 October 2026, the Chief Executive, Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR) pursuant to the provisions of the Acquisition of Land Act 1967, the Transport Infrastructure Act 1994 and the Transport Planning and Coordination Act 1994 issued a notice that intends to take an area of 10 square metres … in the locality of Beenleigh, for a purpose incidental to transport (railway) namely road… Any written objections to the intended take are required by 17 November 2026."

Des Crump is a historian and bottle collector; the reason the latter is important will become clear shortly.

He spoke to Steve Austin about his research into Mr Thorsborne on 612 ABC Brisbane Mornings.

"It's [a] funny little shape, [a] funny little bit of land, but it's surprising that there's no descendants because he [August Thorsborne] had quite a few children," he said.

"It doesn't seem to be specifically connected to where he ran his soft drink business, and he had a brewery, and all those other things that wouldn't fit on that sort of block of land."

Despite the lack of heirs apparent, the family name is still prominent in the areas around Holmview station, with a road and a park named after the family.

The talented Mr Thorsborne

Mr Crump, who has roles at The University of Queensland and the State Archives, has some of the bottles from the soft drink company in his collection.

"(The Thorsborne family) came out from Sweden, ended up in Beenleigh in the 1870s, had interests in the hotel area, mostly known for his soft drink factory," he said.

"It was a Beenleigh Soda with this gauntlet trademark."

He said the bottles in his collection were rare because the early ones had marbles in them and children would break them to get to them.

Mr Thorsborne was also a member of the Beenleigh Shire Council in 1888.

Mr Crump said Mr Thorsborne had 11 children, two died in childhood, and the family had the soft drink factory through to the 1930s.

"So, you think there must still be family there," he said.

A Department of Transport and Main Roads spokesperson said it had released an updated design for the Holmview station precinct as part of Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail.

"The updated design of the Logan and Gold Coast Faster Rail (LGC) project includes upgrades to local roads and a new road connection from Spanns Road to Thorsborne Street," the spokesperson said.

"Anyone who believes they may have an interest in the August Thorsborne estate or the land is encouraged to contact TMR."

title: Commercial rock lobster fisheries closed due to antibiotic trade risk
text:
Commercial rock lobster and dive fisheries in parts of Tasmania's south-east will stay closed for three months to "mitigate trade risks" linked to antibiotic use by the salmon industry.

The Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) has issued two notices declaring certain commercial areas closed from November 15 this year to February 14 next year.

The commercial taking of rock lobster and the setting of rock lobster pots will not be allowed within parts of the Southern Channel "Therapeutic Management Area" (TMA).

The new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline. (ABC News: Bec Pridham)

Commercial divers will not be allowed to take short-spined sea urchins, long-spined sea urchins and periwinkles in the Northern Channel TMA.

The notice for commercial divers says the closure is "part of the arrangements to mitigate trade risks associated with aquaculture therapeutant use."

Tassal is one of three major salmon producers with pens in Tasmanian waterways. (Bob Brown Foundation)

NRE last month released its Wild Fisheries Market Access Plan ahead of the planned use of antibiotics to treat a bacterial disease that caused mass deaths in salmon farms over the past two summers.

Under the plan, wild fisheries near salmon pens treated with antibiotics get temporarily closed.

This is done to avoid the risk of antibiotic detections in wild seafood that could trigger export bans by countries with zero tolerance.

The industry has struggled with mass deaths of fish during recent summers. (Supplied: Bob Brown Foundation)

Closures linked to use of oxytetracycline by Tassal

The new closures are linked to salmon company Tassal's recent use of the antibiotic oxytetracycline (OTC) at its salmon farms at Great Taylors Bay and Meads Creek in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel.

A map showing the areas of the rock lobster fishery that will be closed from Sunday. (ABC News: Hamed Akrami)

"This localised, temporary closure is a precaution to protect export market access in an area accounting for approximately 1.6 per cent of Tasmania's annual historical rock lobster catch," a Tassal spokesperson said.

Tassal has been administering OTC by injection, rather than orally through medicated food.

The industry has lost large amounts of fish stocks to disease recently. (Huon)

When it first started using the antibiotic last month, the Department of Health said it posed no risk to the public.

"Public Health has confirmed swimming and recreational fishing remain completely safe," the Tassal spokesperson said.

"We recognise the consequences for any affected commercial rock lobster fishers and are working with the wild fisheries sector on appropriate support, with monitoring underway to support reopening as soon as possible."

The industry has been adminstering the antibiotic via injection. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Salmon Tasmania, which represents the state's three main salmon companies, has separately applied for an emergency permit to use the antibiotic florfenicol to treat the bacterial disease.

The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA) is currently seeking public submissions about the application, with a decision likely this month.

The salmon industry received an emergency permit to use florfenicol late last year, but it was revoked in March this year after florfenicol was detected in wild seafood more than 10 kilometres away.

In a statement, an NRE spokesperson said it was a "precautionary closure, in line with the Aquaculture Therapeutant Wild Fisheries Market Access Management Plan, designed to protect market access for Tasmania's wild fisheries and was not related to any food safety concern".

Salmon in a fish farm enclosure. (Supplied: Tassal)

Industry interests 'trample' those of wild fisheries, MP says

Franklin independent MP Peter George said he was shocked at the closure.

"I am hearing from outraged fishers appalled at the closure and its impact on their livelihoods — and expressing concern about transiting through or anchoring in these waters when they're using seawater to keep their catch alive," he said.

"There's now no question that the multinational salmon industry's interests trample over those of Tasmania's wild fishers", he added.

title: ANZ boss warns global markets in 'dangerous situation' as interest rates rise
text:
The head of ANZ says he sees a "dangerous situation" with global markets.

Nuno Matos, ANZ's chief executive, says the competition for capital is intense globally, driven by the AI and data centre build-out, which is feeding an expenditure super-cycle.

He says the combination of that race for capital, the prevailing level of government expenditure, higher and stubborn inflation and rising interest rates are a serious problem.

Which debt crisis will hit first? Technology and artificial intelligence have enthralled investors, and Australia's super funds have dived in with their ears pinned back. But now comes the reckoning.

"Globally, undoubtedly, the combination of those four factors, and Australia is not different in that regard," he said today.

"They are contributing to a competition for capital. We never saw this amount of spending in our lives, in our lifetimes.

"We have a very curious situation in the world where we have equity markets at record highs, basically because of the tech wave and basically because of the AI wave, but at the same time you have record highs of interest rates.

" It's a dangerous situation for the world. "

Mr Matos was giving evidence at a parliamentary inquiry in Canberra. The chief executives of Australia's big four banks will appear before the inquiry.

Global shock could hit Australia's economy

Mr Matos said he did not think Australia was heading for recession.

He said he was expecting Australia's economy to slow down noticeably in the near future, but he did not think it would contract.

Nuno Matos says he is not expecting Australia's economy to suffer a homegrown recession. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Last week, Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said something similar. She said the RBA was not forecasting a recession for Australia.

However, Mr Matos said it was possible that Australia could be hit by a negative global shock, linked to the AI build-out and intense global competition for capital, which would cause serious economic problems in Australia.

Is the Firmus fiasco a crack in the AI boom? Amidst the wreckage of last week's failed mega capital-raising by data centre provider Firmus Technologies was a creeping sense that, once again, Australia had somehow fallen short.

"There is much more risk, at this point in time, for that scenario coming from outside," he said.

"If we have an AI, let's call it an AI blip, in the world, we will have globally a big problem.

"Now, do I expect that? No. But that's not impossible to happen."

He said so much capital was being invested in data centres and AI-linked industries and companies that things could get very "complicated" if that process was derailed.

Ed Husic speaks to Nuno Matos about AI. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Interest rates are at a 18-year high Tell us how this will impact your livelihood or business here

Government spending adding to inflation

Simon Kennedy, Liberal MP and deputy chair of the committee, asked Mr Matos if government spending was too high and contributing to Australia's battle with inflation.

Mr Matos said any spending reduction in the economy, "public or private", would take pressure off inflation. But he said high inflation was a global phenomenon at the moment and it was the consequence of several trends.

The US midterms should scare the heck out of Albanese A hasty fix that crashes the economy might quicken Labor's march to a Trumpocalypse of its own making.

He said the huge global investment in renewables, the huge growth in defence spending, and the massive spend on AI infrastructure were creating large capacity pressures for economies.

He said all governments should be reflecting on how they competed for capital.

"Today, governance and administrations in the world, they compete fiercely for capital, especially long-term capital," he said.

"Every time the administration goes to the market, they are now competing with AI infrastructure, which also demands long-term capital. This is creating inflation.

Local politics of data centres The US midterms show that the technological gold rush of AI could quickly become an electoral liability

"Undoubtedly, less spending in general will contribute to lower inflation, and that would contribute to a lower interest rate environment if we had less spending."

Mr Matos said there were times during the economic cycle, such as during recessions, when it was right for governments to "jump in and support the economy."

But, he said, over the longer term the private sector should lead investment and spending "to make an economy sustainable".

Mr Kennedy asked: "So we really need to see a rebalancing of that equation [in Australia at the moment]?"

Mr Matos said that would be a positive thing.

"I think everybody would love to have an equation where private capital leads investment and spending," he said.

However, he did not nominate where he thought governments should cut spending.

Nuno Matos says AI could bring a lot of benefits but it also has a "dark side". (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

AI has a 'dark side'

On the topic of AI, Mr Matos also warned about the dangers of pushing ahead with a widespread adoption of AI without "guardrails" and "global regulation".

"AI has a dark side," he told MPs.

"AI can be used maliciously to [commit] fraud, to defraud customers, to scam customers, to impact critical infrastructure, being bank infrastructure, public infrastructure. That's very obvious.

Australia to pursue AI guardrails after OpenAI breach OpenAI's delayed reporting of an autonomous agent breaching a government website has strengthened Australia's push for tougher AI safety and disclosure rules.

"Which means that going into a wide adoption of AI without having the adequate guardrails, it's a big problem.

"[And] on the job side, I can't tell you if AI will have a net positive, net negative, or neutral impact on jobs in the world, or in Australia.

"I can't tell you because if I tell you, I will be speculating.

"I can only bring the following rationale. In the past, all technologies that were found in the world actually supported more employment and more growth. Until today, that has been the trend.

"The question is if AI will be different, meaning if some of those [warnings] we listen to, [for example], that AI will kill 50 per cent of jobs happen, [then we] will have a crisis and it's not going to be in Australia [only], it's going to be a global crisis.

"This is one of the few examples where I would say some global regulation is needed to make sure that society does not [get] into trouble."

Boss defends ANZ's $7.6b profit

ANZ recently posted a full-year cash profit of $7.59 billion.

Committee chair, Labor MP Ed Husic, asked how much that profit had increased on last year's result.

"It's up 31 per cent on a reported basis. On a real basis it's up 10 per cent," Mr Matos replied.

ANZ posts $7.3b profit The ASX eked out a marginal gain with miners cushioning losses in the banks and property sectors.

The bank's statutory profit was $7.3 billion, up 23 per cent on the year.

Mr Husic said everyone in Australia seemed to be going through tough times at the moment except for Australia's biggest businesses.

Mr Matos defended the operation of Australia's big banks. He said they were "performing their role in delivering to society".

"The mortgage business is one of the least profitable businesses in banking in Australia, and it has reduced profitability year after year, at least in the last 20 years," he said.

title: No answers on contaminated Defence site being remediated before hand-back
text:
The federal government has been unable to say whether it will remediate heavy fuels and PFAS chemicals from a former Navy fuel storage base in Darwin city centre before it returns the land to Larrakia custodians.

The defence and finance ministers announced on Monday the government would give the former Stokes Hill Navy fuel storage site to the Larrakia people as part of its national divestment of more than 60 Defence sites to both raise and save money.

The 3.8 hectare site behind Stokes Hill Wharf was the Navy's main fuel storage base for its ships in Darwin from 1920, until seven of the 11 fuel tanks were destroyed by the Japanese bombing of Darwin in 1942.

The site, near Darwin city, hasn't been used since 2014. (ABC News: Mitch Abram)

The defence department stopped using the site in 2014 and declared it surplus to its requirements the following year.

The ABC understands the federal government has offered to return the site to the Larrakia Nation Aboriginal corporation.

Some Larrakia custodians, including Lorraine Williams, welcomed the offer to return the land, which contains a registered tawny frogmouth sacred site.

"For a long time, that defence force area of land, we've fought for it, our old people have fought for those lands," she said.

But in 2017 Defence studies found PFAS — a chemical from firefighting foam now banned on Defence facilities — in the groundwater at the site, as well as fuel contamination from the old tanks.

Larrakia custodian Lorraine Williams wants the Stokes Hill site remediated before it is returned. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

Ms Williams said the federal government needed to clean both up before handing the site back.

"Hopefully the area will be remediated, as with the other areas Defence have handed back to Larrakia over on the Cox Peninsula," she said.

In 2015, before the Kenbi Cox Peninsula hand back, the federal government spent $30 million cleaning up asbestos and heavy metals from its former communications sites there.

Asked by the ABC if it would remediate the Stokes Hill land, the defence department said "the management of any site contamination and remediation requirements will be considered through the divestment process".

Four of the fuel tanks survived the Japanese bombing of Darwin in 1942. (ABC News: Mitch Abram)

It also said it "will engage with Northern Territory authorities and traditional owners" about that.

Former communications base earmarked for housing

The federal government also announced a much bigger site, its 362 hectare former Kowandi North communications base at Howard Springs, south of Darwin, will be developed for housing.

NT Chamber of Commerce CEO Glen Hingley said while Darwin's business community welcomed the plan, they still had questions.

Glen Hingley says more housing is needed for Darwin to help local industries expand. (ABC News: Jane Bardon)

"If they do divest this land it's important they sit down with the Northern Territory government, traditional owners and communities around this block to make sure that we have an agreed pathway, if we are going to go ahead with it, to make sure it's done in the best interests of the local area, the local environment and the broader community," Mr Hingley said.

Northern Territory Housing Minister Steve Edgington also requested more information about the proposed housing site.

"We're uncertain of the detail, whether that land will be handed to the Northern Territory government," he said.

Steve Edgington says the NT government wants more information on the plans. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Some Larrakia custodians have asked the government to move the 800-house development planned for Darwin's Lee Point to Kowandi North.

But the Commonwealth said both sites will host housing estates.

Asked by the ABC whether the federal government or a private company will build the Kowandi North housing, a Finance Department spokeswoman said: "The divestment pathway for Kowandi North is still being considered by government, with the future use of the site to support increased housing supply in Darwin.

"The final disposal arrangements remain subject to government consideration."

title: 'If they're winning, we're winning': Suppliers on David Jones closures
text:
While news of David Jones's plans to close half of its stores may sadden some customers, some suppliers say a streamlined operation could boost sales by attracting more shoppers into fewer, higher-performing stores.

The 188-year-old department store went into administration last week.

On Wednesday, its receivers announced plans to close 19 of its 38 stores.

Owner of Spice brand Lord and Lion, Eresha De Zoysa, whose products have been stocked across the David Jones network for five years, said she was concerned the closures would wipe out a significant amount of her business.

"The way that we were able to access people in communities that we ordinarily would not be able to access was by David Jones," she said.

"So even though, on the whole, those stores may not make commercial sense for Anchorage to keep or David Jones to keep … our brand did really well, and we were successful in those stores.

"It's a sad day, but I think we just have to be a bit more clever in how we're going to access [those customers]."

Eresha De Zoysa says she is grateful to be stocked in David Jones. (Supplied)

Documents seen by the ABC show an uncertain future for suppliers that have been asked to continue supplying the store despite unpaid debts.

Ms De Zoysa, a former corporate lawyer who has worked in administration and previously advised David Jones, said she had no doubt a restructured David Jones would succeed and thrive.

"I do hope that the suppliers find a way to renegotiate an outcome with David Jones to continue supplying into the future because it is actually those brands that make David Jones worthwhile," she said.

David Jones 'could not continue operating'

McGrath Nicol has been appointed administrator for David Jones, but separately FTI Consulting has been appointed as receiver for the company's biggest lender, Hilco.

An email sent to suppliers from David Jones chief executive Erica Berchtold, seen by the ABC, said the store portfolio was "no longer the right shape for the business" and the change was about "creating a network that is financially sustainable for the future."

It said the last day of trade for the 19 stores marked for closure was anticipated for later in the year, with the stores expected to continue trading through the peak seasonal period.

David Jones will close 19 of its 38 locations. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

"The business could not continue operating as it was. We had a plan to reset the business, and we still have a plan to reset the business," the email said.

Carlos Martins, owner of men's fashion brand Coast Clothing, said the store closures were the "right way forward".

"Fewer stores will be better for me in the long term," he said.

"Loyal customers will likely shift to online shopping, which will bring greater exposure to my brand, compared to instore where we didn't have a presence."

Slow Down Studios owner Jacob Leung. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Jacob Leung, owner of handwoven blankets business Slowdown Studio, which is not stocked in the closing stores, said although the news was sad, it was good for suppliers.

"It's going to have a massive impact on all of those employees, as well as the communities of the stores that are closing down," he said.

"We only want the best for David Jones because if they're winning, that means we're winning.

"At the end of the day though, it's clear that the business model that David Jones currently operates in is not working, and that's why we are all in this situation."

Focus needs to shift to service

David Jones in Claremont in Perth's Western Suburbs is one of the stores continuing to trade. (ABC News: Zahra Anwary)

Mahala Joyce, co-founder and director of distribution business Over The Fence, has organised pop-ups in David Jones flagship stores for international brands, including Bellroy and Topologie.

Like other suppliers, he said he had negotiated 14-day settlement terms that came with a 5.75 per cent discount. Yet across three purchase orders over six months, he said none was paid on time, while the discount was still applied. Relevant documents have been seen by the ABC.

"Essentially the way that their system is set up is it's set up that those discounts are applied at the start, prior to any payment date," he said.

"It's a systemic flaw."

Mr Joyce said the decision to close David Jones stores was the right move.

David Jones suppliers in limbo Documents seen by ABC News show the unclear situation facing suppliers after the 188-year-old retailer was plunged into voluntary administration this week.

"It's surprising that no-one within their leadership saw that that was a thing that they should have done prior," he said.

"It was broadly known that there were a number of locations, about 19, that were loss-making. And a lot of the people that I spoke to in that business thought that if they had 12 stores in the long run, that that would be a very solid business for them to be able to kind of go forward with."

However, he said David Jones needed to focus on fixing its customer service.

"They can close stores, they can repair relationships with vendors, but until they actually start delivering on the promise, like the service promise that their brand has developed in Australia, even with the store closures, I think it's going to be a tough market for them.

"But if they can deliver on those promises that consumers expect from them, then I think they can be a really strong player in the retail landscape."

title: Addo-Carr free to leave Eels as club rejects extension opportunity
text:
Josh Addo-Carr is free to leave Parramatta immediately after the Eels advised the former Test winger the club would not offer him a contract extension beyond 2027.

After a series of bizarre twists and turns, the Eels have decided Addo-Carr is not wanted after next season and he can start hunting for a new NRL club.

The development comes despite the NRL integrity unit clearing the 31-year-old to return to Parramatta after failing a roadside random drugs test in October.

The ex-NSW State of Origin and Kangaroos star received an unexpected lifeline when his B sample came back negative earlier this month.

"The Parramatta Eels would like to provide an update regarding Josh Addo-Carr following a driving incident in September," an Eels statement read on Thursday.

"After reviewing all relevant information, including the negative result of the B sample, the club has cleared Josh in relation to the issues raised following the incident.

"The NRL has also confirmed it will not be taking any further action, and the club now considers the matter closed.

"Separately, the club has informed Josh and his management that it will not be seeking to extend his current contract beyond the end of the 2027 season."

The Eels will keep the door ajar for Addo-Carr to see out his 2027 contract, but will not stand in his way if he secures a new contract with a rival club.

The 31-year-old is due back at pre-season training with the Eels next week, as his management looks to secure the flyer a future elsewhere.

title: Farmer who's 'not a great swimmer' hopes to be first to swim the Darling
text:
Stroke by stroke, kilometre by kilometre, Scott Gladman has spent the past 72 days consecutively swimming down the Darling River in outback New South Wales.

The 64-year-old Victorian farmer has firmly set his sights on being the first person to swim the river from top to bottom as part of his "Fight the Current" campaign.

He and his support team are well past the halfway mark on their 1,650-kilometre odyssey.

Scott Gladman is taking just over three months to swim 1,650km from Brewarrina to Wentworth. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

Mr Gladman has even surprised himself by what he has achieved so far, having previously never swum more than 8 kilometres in a single stretch, a feat made all the more impressive by a heart scare in 2017 that required a triple stent.

"I'm not a great swimmer but, yeah, [I] love water," he said.

"I thought there'd be some stage where I hit a wall … get really sore or lots of aches and pains … but I've been really lucky, everything's been great."

His determination has been unsurprising to those around him including his wife, George Gladman.

Scott Gladman's wife, George, says there was no talking her husband out of undertaking the enormous swim. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"I couldn't talk him out of it, so I just thought I've got to get on board," she said.

"I suggested a few other things and some other rivers … then I realised there was no changing his mind."

Massive swim 'nothing' compared to mates' ordeal

Mr Gladman's journey is not just a physical pursuit; the 64-year-old's goal is to raise money and awareness for both Motor Neurone Disease and Parkinson's.

His mission was in response to his long-term mate Russ Worldle being diagnosed with Parkinson's, and the separate MND diagnosis of 36-year-old family friend Pat Russell.

Mr Gladman said swimming the length of the Darling was "nothing" compared to what his mates and their families were going through.

Scott Gladman is supported by a rotating team of paddlers, boat drivers and other staff. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"It's nothing to swim down the river … 16, 17, 18 [thousand kilometres] … [and] a little bit of pain you might feel," he said.

Scott and George Gladman, and the whole Fight the Current team, have been overwhelmed by the generosity of people following along the journey.

This includes the remote station owners living along the Darling River, who have accommodated them with places to sleep, cook and clean.

"They would give their shirt right off their back for you; it's been absolutely unbelievable," Mr Gladman said.

This included sizeable donations from the tiny towns along the way in the name of MND and Parkinson's.

The Fight the Current campaign is raising money for Motor Neurone Disease and Parkinson's. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

In Louth, which has a population of roughly 70 people, locals donated $3,700. In the district of Tilpa, with a population of roughly 40, locals pitched in $4,000.

"You go to Bourke, and they raise money … the people out here [are] just fantastic," Mr Gladman said.

The Fight the Current campaign is just $15,000 short of its $150,000 fundraising target.

But as Mr Gladman makes clear, it is not just about raising funds for those battling MND and Parkinson's.

"It's about raising awareness of the plight that these people have out in the bush," he said.

The 1,650km journey will take just over three months from start to finish line. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

" If I can just swim down the river and make one person feel like they're not caring for a loved one by themselves, well, I've done my job. "

Not a solo journey

While Mr Gladman is the face of the swim, gliding down the river — he has a rotating team of paddlers, boat drivers, drivers and other support staff accompanying him.

He credited the team with getting him this far.

Scott Gladman says his swim would not be possible without the support of his team. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

"To a degree I feel guilty … I jump in the water and, to some people, may get all the glory," he said.

"[But] with[out] all these people in the background, it just wouldn't happen."

Support paddler Mike Bremers travelled from Canberra to assist the swim. Having kayaked the Darling before himself, he was responsible for spotting snags and other obstacles in the river.

Mike Bremers is one of a team of people assisting Scott Gladman's swim. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"[Scott] said he needed a support paddler and I thought, 'Yeah, I'd give it a go,'" Mr Bremer said.

"Scott's amazing because he … just goes on all day swimming."

Having fun is the secret

For Mr Gladman and the rest of the team, the marathon journey "has got to be fun" no matter what.

Scott Gladman fuelling up ahead of his day's swim. (ABC Broken Hill: Em Jensen)

This included more than a few frothies at the conclusion of each day's swim.

"I think that's the secret … it's got to be fun, as soon as it becomes a chore, you're in trouble," Mr Gladman said.

His cousin Brian "Tubby" Gladman is in charge of driving Scott and the on-river support team to and from camp each morning and night.

Barring catastrophe, he had little doubt they would reach Wentworth in December.

Brian Gladman is in charge of driving Scott and his support team to and from camp each day. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"He's just a positive mind all the time, [saying] 'If I'm gonna do it, I'm gonna do it,' [and] don't worry, he'll get there," he said.

title: Community preschools in NSW oppose move towards more children, fewer staff
text:
Sarah Kearney sends her daughter to a community preschool on the NSW far south coast, and says the care she receives there is "exceptional".

The 42-year-old mother of two said a high staff-to-student ratio at the Moruya Preschool Kindergarten was a key factor.

"The staff pick up on any signs that she might need extra support," she said.

"They're there to support us parents, and they watch all the children really closely, which I think is what parents want."

A group of protesters in Nowra last week called for the funding program to be scrapped. (ABC News: Grace Crivellaro)

But there are fears that situation could change when the NSW government introduces a new funding model next year.

The Universal Funding Program will actually increase funding for community preschools from $540 million to $625 million, but individual centres will have to take on more enrolments to maximise their share.

Last week NSW Education Minister Prue Car urged community preschools to take in an extra 10,000 students across the state.

She suggested they use a ratio of one staff member for every 10 children.

Prue Car says it is safe to expand staff to child ratios to one to 10. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

"What a lot of these community preschools are saying is that they're full based on the ratios that they want to have, one to three or one to four," Ms Car said.

" We're saying you can expand those ratios to one in 10. It's still safe. "

There are 710 community preschools in NSW, funded primarily through government grants and subsidies, which are supplemented by parent-paid fees and local fundraising.

They differ from public preschools, which are operated by the NSW government, and commercial operators.

Community preschools are run by volunteer parent management committees, are not-for-profit, and have a particular focus on catering to all children with diverse abilities and backgrounds.

Educators are angered by the 2027 Universal Preschool Funding program. (ABC News: Grace Crivellaro)

An e-petition highlighting concerns about the new funding model has garnered more than 40,000 signatures after being launched by staff at Mittagong Community Preschool on November 2.

Families and directors of not-for-profit centres have rallied across the state, including in Sydney, Nowra, Lismore, Queanbeyan and Coffs Harbour, with another protest held on Thursday outside NSW Parliament.

Sleepless nights

Among the protesters in Nowra was Sharon O'Brien from the Lyrebird Preschool, who used a funding estimate calculator published by the NSW Department of Education to gauge the effect of the change.

"We are $100,000 short on operational expenses that have been allocated under this new funding model," she said.

"We take well above our proportion of children with support needs, Aboriginal children with disadvantaged, who we actually financially support by enabling them not to pay fees at all.

"Myself and my team have had many sleepless nights since the data from the funding calculator has come out."

The director of the Keiraville Community Preschool in Wollongong, Margaret Gleeson, said it operated with a ratio of one staff member for every seven children.

Margaret Gleeson fears she will be forced to cut staff as a result of the new funding model. (ABC News: Grace Crivellaro)

She said the centre was licensed by the NSW Early Learning Commission for a maximum of 40 children per day, based on an assessment of environment, equipment, and staffing.

"If I go over my 40 children a day, even by one person, I'm breaching the law. I can be fined," Ms Gleeson said.

" We've been operating since 1952 and I'm scared that unless this funding model changes, that in 2028, we won't be able to open our doors. "

Keiraville Community Preschool was founded by three mothers 74 years ago. (ABC News: Grace Crivellaro)

NSW Greens MP Abigail Boyd, who chaired the Inquiry into Early Childhood Education and Care, said not-for-profit community preschools were known for providing high-quality early education.

"What I found in the inquiry was that amongst all of the really shocking stories of incidents happening in the sector, there was a really good story in there too, and that was community preschools," she said.

"Because they're not-for-profit, they often take the children with additional needs that other for-profit centres won't."

According to a report by the Australian Children's Education and Care Quality Authority, 75 per cent of community preschools were rated as exceeding in the National Quality Standard, compared to the 25 per cent of early childhood education and care services run by commercial operators.

More than 100 protesters gathered outside South Coast MP Liza Butler's office in Nowra last week. (ABC News: Grace Crivellaro)

Community preschool directors and parents have argued that imposing a ratio of one to 10 would compromise those standards.

"The bare minimum ratio is not quality," Jamberoo Preschool director Belinda Hibbert told a 100-strong rally in Nowra last week.

"Take more children, they say, but we're already maximising spaces and are still full with waiting lists."

The education minister has said "transitional funding" would be available to help centres adapt to the changes.

Ms Car said the directors of centres that did not have the physical space to increase enrolments should contact the Department of Education, so they can be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

title: Cummins to 'respond properly' to Khawaja claims tomorrow
text:
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins is set to break his public silence on the sandpaper scandal after taking time to "better understand" the allegations of ex-teammate Usman Khawaja.

Test captain Cummins announced on social media that he would speak to reporters tomorrow morning at Cricket NSW's headquarters in Sydney.

"Happy to speak with any and all media about the events of this week," Cummins posted today.

"I've taken some time to try and better understand the long list and full extent of Uzzy's allegations so I can respond properly."

Cricket Australia is yet to confirm an official time but Cummins said he would speak at 9:30am AEDT between a training session and the start of day three of NSW's Sheffield Shield clash with South Australia.

Many in Australian cricket circles have been demanding Cummins publicly respond to Khawaja's explosive claims in his book about ball tampering in Australia's Test team.

Khawaja told Nine Newspapers of the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the infamous 2018 Test against South Africa in Cape Town: "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."

The retired batter also wrote of Australia's ball tampering in the preceding Ashes Test series against England.

Cummins and fellow fast bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood, and spinner Nathan Lyon, have previously denied knowledge of Australia taking sandpaper onto the Cape Town ground. Starc reiterated that stance on Tuesday.

A writ filed in WA’s Supreme Court has revealed details of Burk Fuel’s alleged fuel-swapping scheme, claiming the petrol chain sold more than four times as much premium 98 than it actually bought and accusing the retailer of tricking customers by secretly filling and mixing premium tanks with cheap regular unleaded. Consumer Protection announced on Monday it was suing Burk Fuel and its director Umar Farooq for allegedly selling 91 fuel that was labelled as 95 and 98 premium products in an alleged breach of Australian Consumer Law. Burk Fuel now have 14 locations around the state. Burk Fuel However, the writ, published in WA’s Supreme Court on Thursday, revealed Consumer Protection was not just suing Burk Fuel, but also its subsidiary trucking company Burk Energy, which was used to ship its fuel. Burk previously advertised its in-house trucking company as a way to cut costs on delivering its fuel, and claimed its 98 fuel – otherwise known as its B-Pro Premium product – would provide customers with “cleaner combustion and superior engine protection”.

Advertisement

“When it matters, trust the fuel that’s built for power,” it said in its advertising materials, according to the writ. However, the writ systemically laid out the basis of the alleged deception, and found the strongest evidence appeared to be discrepancies between what Burk bought through its petrol wholesaler and how much was sold to consumers. Burk has previously indicated it would fight the allegations, but has made no comment following Consumer Protection’s announcement on Monday. Farooq has repeatedly been contacted for comment. The company is due to file a defence at a later date. Consumer Protection obtained figures that found customers paid for nearly 9 million litres of 95 fuel over an eight-month period, between July 2025 and February 2026.

Advertisement

However, the writ alleged delivery logs over the course of six months showed not a single litre of 95 was delivered to Burk’s locations. Umar Farooq is the Perth-based director. LinkedIn/Umar Farooq The only delivery recorded was a small batch on January 13 this year, which was only about 8000 litres. According to the writ, rather than being put in the 95 underground tanker to be sold appropriately, it was dumped mistakenly into the Burk Mount Lawley site’s 98 tank. However, as a result of the minuscule purchase figure over seven months, Consumer Protection said it would ultimately allege Burk misrepresented its 91 fuel as 95. Relating to Burk’s premium 98 fuel, it also found customers paid for more than 7 million litres at the pump over the same seven-month time frame.

Advertisement

However, the writ alleged Burk had only ever bought 1.69 million litres of it across the course of Consumer Protection’s investigation. Related Article Consumer rights Perth’s cheapest petrol chain faces prosecution over claims it passed off 91 fuel as premium Consumer Protection alleged Burk did not buy any 98 fuel for the month of July 2025, but continued to sell it at the pumps. The watchdog alleged Burk bought 14.7 million litres of regular 91 fuel to make up the difference and mixed the fuels. This would mean any motorist who filled up either received mixed fuel or 91, the writ alleged. The lawsuit revealed Consumer Protection’s investigators found out about the discrepancies between what was sold and what was purchased after discovering a WhatsApp group allegedly run by the company’s truck fleet manager, who is understood to have now left the country.

Advertisement

Burk’s truck fleet was run in-house, and the writ alleged the fleet manager would set out explicit instructions over the messaging app and order drivers to log every delivery on paper dockets. All up, customers would have bought more than 50 million litres of unleaded petrol across the period Consumer Protection investigated. Using Thursday’s reported prices for Burk stations on FuelWatch, this would mean the company could have claimed upwards of $2 million on top of its regular profit. The company is currently under investigation by authorities for its fuel quality. Burk Fuel In the writ, Consumer Protection said it would ask WA’s Supreme Court, if its case was proven, to consider disqualifying Farooq from managing corporations in the future, and for him and the business to pay financial penalties for allegedly breaching Australian Consumer Law.

Advertisement

The lawsuit claimed Farooq had intimate knowledge of the alleged scheme because he was the sole director of Burk, the trucking company, and the fact he dealt with the supplier responsible for ensuring fuel allocations were available for the drivers to collect. Related Article Exclusive

Courts Perth’s cheapest petrol chain hauls landlords to court over eviction notices Consumer Protection alleged Farooq was involved in the load plan discussions on WhatsApp, and he regularly notified FuelWatch about his prices on the wrong products. “At all material times Mr Farooq was knowingly concerned in Burk and Burk Fuel’s conduct in that he knew that fuel was being offered and supplied to consumers at the retail fuel outlets as PULP 95 and as PULP 98, knew that the Instagram statements, website statements, FuelWatch notifications, price board statements and bowser statements were being made, and knew that the fuel so offered and supplied had a RON [research octane number] lower than the represented minimum RON for that grade,” the writ said. Consumer Protection said it would also seek for the court to ban Burk Fuel and Farooq from selling fuel in WA for a period of five years, and pay back consumers.

Advertisement

The company has not yet responded to the claims.

Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner has pushed for a new train station at the gateway to Brisbane Airport, arguing for improved public transport links to a precinct currently locked out of Brisbane Metro services by longstanding contractual restrictions. Speaking at a BNE Enterprise business breakfast on Thursday, Schrinner and Brisbane Airport chief executive Gert-Jan de Graaff both lamented Airtrain’s 35-year exclusive contract, which monopolised public transport to the airport terminals. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner and Brisbane Airport Corporation chief executive Gert-Jan de Graaff have lamented the transport challenges at the airport. Cameron Atfield While it has long been a bugbear for travellers – particularly since the previous Labor state government introduced 50¢ fares everywhere else on the network – it has also meant airport precinct workers had to pay more to get to and from work than their neighbours. Under the terms of the contract, the UK-based Universities Superannuation Scheme-owned Airtrain charges an inflated price – currently $23.30 from Central Station – to travellers using the service.

Advertisement

Airtrain offered a discounted fare for airport precinct workers through a $48 weekly ticket. Assuming a five-day working week, those workers would only pay $5 a week if Airtrain was part of the Translink 50¢ fare scheme. USS Axle, a subsidiary of USS, acquired Airtrain and its concession in 2013. That concession, now in its final decade, will expire on May 5, 2036, at which point the Airport line will be subject to the same fares as the rest of south-east Queensland’s train network. “The problem is, fundamentally, that the Airtrain primarily serves visitors, but it’s a growing area that needs transport services for the people that work here, and so that’s the problem that we need to solve,” Schrinner said. Airport staff pay significantly more to commute than those working elsewhere in Brisbane. “And so, what is the solution? Metro could well be the solution, and we’re doing the business case on that right now. But there could be other solutions to that problem as well.

“One thing that comes to mind is well, what if additional stations were added into Airtrain that accommodate workers as well? “We’re pretty successful in developing a route network in the air, but that only works if people can get to it from the airport as well on the ground,” he said. Related Article Exclusive

Brisbane Airport Adidas to open first Australian airport store in Brisbane De Graaff said he was in constant dialogue with the Queensland government about how the Airtrain concession could be modified to reduce train fares and allow for metro services to the airport. “We [want to] get that metro not only going to Skygate, Terminal 1 and Terminal 2, previously known as the International Terminal and Domestic Terminal, but also to the future Terminal 3,” he said. title: See the full list: The suburbs where home prices have grown as much as 417 per cent
text:
In Brief Median sale prices have doubled from metropolitan Sydney and Darwin through to coastal cities and regional towns.

Suburbs along the east coast represent the largest growth in value for houses and units.

In 2011, Australia's property market was valued at around $4.2 trillion.

Fifteen years later, it's worth more than $12 trillion, according to the latest update from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

But growth in property value has varied largely due to lifestyle factors and development booms, analysis by real estate advertiser REA Group on prices since 2011 shows.

In Pokolbin, in NSW's Hunter Valley region, the median house price in 2011 was $315,000. Now, it sits at $1,628,000, having risen 417 per cent.

Rounding out the top 10 behind Pokolbin, the suburbs with the largest growth in median sale prices for houses across the country are Jordan Springs (NSW), Palm Beach (NSW), Byron Bay (NSW), Mermaid Waters (QLD), Bellamack (NT), Boolaroo (NSW), Buddina (QLD), Miami (QLD) and Forde (ACT).

How about units?

The east coast also leads the top suburbs for units.

The largest growth has been in Palm Beach (QLD), Bogangar (NSW), Tugun (QLD), Jindabyne (NSW), Miami (QLD), Reedy Creek (QLD), Mona Vale (NSW), Currumbin Waters (QLD), Double Bay (NSW) and Casuarina (NSW).

In the Gold Coast's Palm Beach, the median sale price for a unit is $1.2 million, an increase of 260 per cent from its value 15 years ago. Similar growth has been seen in suburbs along the Gold Coast.

The Northern Territory tended to record smaller price growth for units than for houses, with the top suburb increasing 26 per cent over the period.

READ MORE Buying a unit is cheaper than renting in this inner-city spot

Trends across the country

From metropolitan Sydney and Darwin to coastal cities and regional towns, median sale prices have doubled in dozens of suburbs over the last 15 years.

Megan Lieu, a senior economic analyst at REA Group, says several factors have driven this growth.

"One of the key factors has been the lower cash rates seen throughout 2012-2021," she told SBS News.

"Borrowing capacities increased, resulting in higher demand from buyers and significant growth in home prices."

The majority of suburbs in the top 10 are in NSW and Queensland.

Lifestyle factors have also been a major driver.

"Any beachside, coastal and tree-change suburbs saw strong growth in the past 15 years as well," Lieu said.

"With Australia's population ageing, many retirees or older Australians have also migrated to Queensland, in particular the Richmond–Tweed, Sunshine Coast and Gold Coast regions where lifestyle and community meet."

There has been strong interstate migration, with many residents from NSW and Victoria choosing to move to Queensland in particular.

For other suburbs, their recent development contributes to the growth, such as Jordan Springs, which was only officially registered in 2011.

In the Northern Territory, suburbs like Bellamack and Johnston have jumped much higher than the rest of the state, with 313 per cent and 260 per cent growth respectively. The next highest suburb grew in value by 69 per cent.

"With affordability becoming more challenged, many Australians have moved away from metro areas, where homes tend to cost more," Lieu said.

"This has driven strong population growth in regional areas and higher rates of growth in these areas compared to capital cities. Unsurprisingly, the majority of the top 10 growth suburbs nationally were located in regional areas."

title: Facing fossil fuel criticism, Albanese urges world not to overlook Pacific climate plight
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese has called for nations to support the Pacific Resilience Facility initiative, launched in 2025.

UN secretary-general António Guterres railed against the oil and gas lobby during his speech at COP31.

World leaders have been urged to extend a lifeline to Pacific nations under threat from rising sea levels and extreme weather at the COP31 summit in Türkiye.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese issued the call to action on Wednesday at the opening of the two-day World Leaders Climate Action Summit segment of the United Nations event.

Australia will lead negotiations at the annual climate talks and Albanese said it would use the opportunity to highlight the plight of its regional neighbours.

"We sought this role because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family," he said.

He also called for nations to support the Pacific Resilience Facility, launched in 2025 and designed to raise $US500 million ($726 million) for climate change and adaptation projects.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I plead with you to join our campaign to help the nations of the Pacific to confront a climate challenge that they certainly did not create," he said.

However, climate activists and politicians have criticised Albanese for failing to directly mention fossil fuels during his speech.

Independent senator David Pocock said that, while Australia has some "good stories" to tell when it comes to adopting renewable energy, more work is needed to reduce Australia's involvement in fossil fuel projects.

"The fact that the prime minister not once mentioned fossil fuels, I think, shows you how captured the major parties are by the fossil fuel industry," Pocock told SBS News.

"They want to be able to talk about the good stuff we're doing, but not the fact that the Albanese government has approved 38 fossil fuel projects, new projects or extensions since they came into office, and that is not compatible with a livable Pacific, let alone what's happening here in Australia."

READ MORE A rare climate milestone arrives as a four-year deadline looms

Pocock said Australia needs to "get real" about weaning itself off of its dependency on fossil fuels.

"This is a huge issue. It's here now. It's only getting worse, unless we see countries like Australia ... the third biggest fossil fuel exporter of the world, come up with a very serious plan going forward around not approving more fossil fuel projects and a planned phase-out."

'The world we know is over'

Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine, whose Pacific nation is threatened by rising sea levels, said: "Every new oil well drilled, every new piece of coal extracted is a threat to my country's future."

"The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear," she said.

Heine also warned of the dire threat posed by overshooting the 2015 Paris Agreement to hold "the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels" and pursue efforts "to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels".

"It's time to wake up," said Heine. "Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over."

Outgoing United Nations secretary-general António Guterres also addressed attendees, calling for urgent action to address climate change, including phasing out fossil fuels.

His call came months after the UN warned the world was on track to surpass 1.5C of warming within a few years and should act to limit the severity and duration of the overshoot.

"Our first climate duty is to tell the truth, and the brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said.

"The last four years were the hottest ever, and fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet. This is the path of mutually assured destruction."

Greater investments in renewable energy, including solar power, could help nations move away from coal, oil and gas, Guterres said.

"Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs, but that will not happen on its own.

"It's time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction."

title: Finnish president brings Albanese into embassy joke that's swept the world
text:
In brief Finland's Canberra embassy made an innocuous post on its Instagram page earlier this week announcing a one-day closure.

The mundane announcement took on a life of its own, receiving more than 11 million views.

An innocuous social media post by Finland's embassy in Canberra has become an unlikely viral meme, attracting millions of views and reaching the highest levels of government in both countries.

"I have confirmed to the Prime Minister of Australia Anthony Albanese that the Finnish Embassy in Canberra is open," Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a selfie posted with Albanese at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye on Thursday morning AEDT.

The president was referring to an announcement three days earlier by the Finnish embassy in Canberra that it would be closed on Tuesday for a team planning event.

Set to a jaunty piano tune and accompanied by a video of the northern lights, the post was simply a light-hearted public service announcement.

But thanks to the unpredictable nature of social media algorithms, the seemingly mundane announcement took on a life of its own, attracting more than 11 million views on Instagram and hundreds of thousands of likes.

Social media users were quick to embrace the meme, flooding the comments section with tongue-in-cheek responses.

"Bad day to be a Finnish embassy in Canberra enthusiast," one said.

"Is everything ok? Call if you need me," said another.

Other Finnish embassies also joined in on the joke.

"For anyone affected by this closure, the Embassy of Finland in Prague will be open as usual tomorrow," the Czech Republic embassy said.

Finland's ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea, said the embassy was taking the viral moment in its stride.

"We started the planning day quite normally. We went through what a successful year we had this year, all the visits and then how do we build on that for next year," he told ABC News breakfast on Thursday.

"Then people started getting messages like, hang on, there's something happening on Instagram and elsewhere."

He said the response had been overwhelmingly positive.

"Everybody was saying that Finland has never been this big in the news. The other thing, Canberra has never been this big on the market either; maybe it's a positive for everyone," he said.

The embassy followed up with a tongue-in-cheek ribbon-cutting ceremony on Wednesday to mark the reopening.

"After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened after its temporary closure on 10 November 2026," it said on social media.

Previous posts by the page had attracted fewer than 100 likes, but Haapea said the embassy was now attracting real-life visitors.

"Yesterday there was actually a fair bit of traffic outside the embassy, lots of people were coming to take pictures and we put some brochures outside to make sure we spread the Finnish propaganda at the same time. That was all good," he said.

It's not the first time Finland has found itself in the social media spotlight.

Last month, the country's state-owned tourism agency launched a viral campaign inviting 16 singles from around the world to Helsinki for what it billed as the "most epic dinner date".

Called Love at First Bite, the campaign aimed to bring strangers together over a candlelit dinner showcasing Finnish cuisine, with the possibility of finding love.

title: The Australians paying an extra 11 per cent on flight costs
text:
In Brief Regional and remote airfares are regularly more than 10 per cent higher than routes connecting major cities.

Half of regional and remote routes carry fewer than 15,000 passengers a year, with around 10 flights a week.

Even though people flying on regional and remote routes around Australia pay higher airfares than those on city routes, the viability of some of these routes could be at risk.

New analysis has found that regional and remote airfares were 11 per cent higher per customer and 13 per cent higher per kilometre than routes connecting major cities, between 2023 and 2025.

The Productivity Commission has analysed cost and revenue data from airlines for the first time, finding that on some routes, such as short regional and short remote routes, the fare per kilometre was more than double that of city routes.

Many regional and remote routes carry less than 15,000 passengers a year. On average, around 10 flights or fewer each week take off with at least a third of the seats empty.

Competition is also lower, with 90 per cent of passengers using Qantas Group or Virgin Australia.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Meanwhile, high costs and a lack of competition have raised concerns about the future viability of these services.

Why does it cost more to fly regionally?

According to the Productivity Commission's analysis, 91 per cent of regional airfares can be attributed to operating costs. It says the remaining profit margin of nine per cent is broadly comparable to most major city routes.

But on some routes, the profit margins are much higher. Mining routes, on average, are 20 per cent or more.

"When operators have to spread the costs of running flights across a small number of passengers, they’re often choosing between charging higher fares or running them at a loss," commissioner Martin Stokie said.

READ MORE The grim news for Australian travellers quietly updated this week

The Productivity Commission is set to deliver a final report to the government next year, with guidance on how best to support a competitive, reliable and affordable aviation network outside major cities.

Impacts on regional and remote communities

Regional and remote communities can be disproportionately affected, as access to health services, economic opportunities, and connections outside their communities relies on air travel.

Despite potentially limited capacity to pay higher fares, they often have minimal access to alternative transportation options.

"The challenges facing a remote island community are very different to those facing a large regional tourism destination or a mining centre," commissioner Catherine de Fontenay said.

The Productivity Commission said that since higher fares reflect the higher costs operators incur, any support should target people in regional and remote communities trying to access key services.

Short regional and remote routes have been identified as particularly at risk as costs rise, and are often served by a single airline.

Many of these routes earn a profit margin of less than 5 per cent, making them vulnerable to cost increases or reduced demand, the report states.

The operating environment is "challenging" for regional airports, the report found, with many operating at a loss or reliant on government support.

Council-owned airports and aerodromes have an estimated replacement cost of approximately $4 billion, while meeting government regulation was said to increase costs for some operators.

The Productivity Commission said any government intervention should focus on connectivity, particularly for remote areas and islands.

"We spoke to people in communities all around Australia who told us how important air travel is for them," de Fontenay said.

title: The type of homeowners on the rise as fewer Australians take out a mortgage
text:
in brief Australia saw the biggest drop in investor home loans on record in the September quarter.

A greater proportion of owner-occupiers are taking out mortgages.

Rising interest rates and Labor's tax changes have spurred the biggest drop in investor home loans on record, as owner-occupiers claim a greater share of the housing market.

New investor lending fell 30.6 per cent to 35,301 loans in the September quarter, driving a 15 per cent fall in total home loans, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on Wednesday.

While lending to owner-occupiers also fell, the shallower 5.3 per cent decline meant the share of owner-occupiers taking out home loans has climbed to 68 per cent from 59 per cent before the May budget.

Labor has been wary of claiming all the credit for the deepening housing downturn, amid falling consumer and business confidence.

But Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said the rising share of owner-occupiers in the market was a good early indicator that the tax changes were having their intended effect.
